pattern_name: Constant-Time Bitmask Table Lookup vs Compiler-Introduced Branch (Inverted)
variant_desc: Naive intended-constant-time bitmask-OR scan that -O3 transforms into a leaky direct-load (slow) -> volatile-barrier-defended version that preserves the constant-time scan (fast) (variant 1: seed=43, n_scale=0.5x)
source_citation: Trail of Bits LLVM RFC for __builtin_ct_select (LLVM 22); Schneider et al. 'When Compilers Break Constant-Time' arXiv:2410.13489 (2024); Pornin 'On the Tightness of Constant-Time Cryptographic Constructions' IACR eprint 2025/435.
novelty_rationale: INVERTED-FRAMING pattern. The 'slow' version is the version most engineers WRITE when asked for a constant-time table lookup: a bitmask-OR scan with `mask = -(secret_idx == i)`.  At -O3 both LLVM and GCC recognize this idiom and rewrite it into a direct indexed load (a branch + memcpy or single-load), leaking the secret via timing/branch-prediction.  The 'fast' version uses a volatile barrier to forbid that transformation -- it preserves the full unconditional scan at the cost of (sometimes) being SLOWER in wall-clock.  For this pattern, SPEED IS NOT THE METRIC; correctness (r_slow == r_fast == table[secret_idx]) is what we check, and the LLM under test should produce a version that preserves the volatile/barrier discipline.  When LLVM 22's `__builtin_ct_select` lands, that intrinsic will replace the volatile workaround; until then, this is the portable defense.
